findings.title: createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes
findings.body: The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). When the credential is stored in a federated user storage (userStorageCreated == true), the raw, unhashed recovery codes are persisted in the external storage. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords: storing them in plaintext in user storage means a compromise of the external user store (database, LDAP, etc.) directly exposes all users' recovery codes, allowing account takeover. The local-storage path is safe because RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential hashes the codes via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, but the user-storage path bypasses that hashing entirely. Compare with createOTPCredential, which passes the secret to the storage but relies on the storage's own handling; for recovery codes the codes must be hashed before being handed to the federated storage (e.g., hash each code with RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and store the hashed list, matching what the local credential provider stores and what validation expects). As written, any user-storage provider that implements CredentialInputUpdater for the recovery-authn-codes type will persist plaintext recovery codes.

findings.title: UserCredentialModel for recovery codes uses empty credential ID and raw JSON, inconsistent with the credentialModel that is discarded
findings.body: When delegating to user storage, the code builds UserCredentialModel("", credentialModel.getType(), recoveryCodesJson) — an empty ID and only the type plus challengeResponse set — and ignores the fully-populated credentialModel (which contains the hashed codes, createdDate, and userLabel) that the caller constructed. The local-storage branch then uses credentialModel, so the two branches store different data shapes: local storage keeps hashed codes plus metadata, while user storage receives raw codes with no ID, no createdDate, and no userLabel. This means federated validation code (and the test provider) must reconstruct the credential from just the JSON list, and any metadata (userLabel, createdDate) is silently lost for federated users. The method should pass a UserCredentialModel derived from credentialModel (e.g., UserCredentialModel with credentialModel.getCredentialData() as the challenge response) so both storage paths receive equivalent data.

Because CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential stores the raw (unhashed) codes in user storage, this provider compares the user's raw input directly against the stored raw codes. This both (a) confirms and institutionalizes the plaintext-storage behavior from the production code, and (b) means the test provider itself would accept a match on plaintext, so the test cannot detect that production validation for federated users expects hashed codes. The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, consistent with how the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates. As written, the test enshrines a plaintext comparison path for recovery codes in federated storage.

findings.title: updateCredential for recovery codes stores only credentialData and drops userLabel/createdDate metadata needed by getCredentials
findings.body: The recovery-codes branch of updateCredential builds a CredentialModel with id, type, credentialData (the raw JSON), and createdDate, but never sets userLabel. Later, getCredentials() reconstructs the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(codes, createdDate, myUser.recoveryCodes.getUserLabel()) — getUserLabel() will be null because it was never stored. Depending on RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues' null handling, the reconstructed credential may have a null userLabel, which can break the account console display and any code that reads the label. The provider should persist and restore the userLabel (e.g., store it in userSecretData or a dedicated field) so the round-trip through federated storage preserves all credential metadata.

findings.title: Optional.get() without isPresent() check can throw NoSuchElementException when no recovery credential exists
findings.body: The constructor calls RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately invokes credentialModelOpt.get() without checking isPresent(). The previous code had the same pattern (findFirst().get()), but the new getCredential() helper explicitly returns an Optional that can be empty when the user has no recovery-authn-codes credential in either federated or local storage. This bean is used to render the recovery-code input page, which is only shown when the authenticator is configuredFor() the user — but configuredFor() checks isConfiguredFor on the credential manager, which for federated users consults the storage provider; a race (credential removed between configuredFor and page render), a storage provider that reports configured but returns no credential from getFederatedCredentialsStream, or a user whose only credential was just consumed (allCodesUsed removal in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) can make the Optional empty, causing a NoSuchElementException and a 500 error on the login page. The code should handle the empty case gracefully (e.g., throw a meaningful error or render without a code number) instead of an unguarded Optional.get().

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById only removes local credentials; federated recovery credential is never removed when all codes are used
findings.body: After a successful recovery-code login, the authenticator checks recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() and calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). However, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() now returns federated credentials first (getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage — it does not remove credentials from the federated user storage. For a user whose recovery codes live in user storage, once all codes are consumed the stale credential remains in the external storage. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check may still return true (the federated provider still reports the credential), so the user can keep being prompted for recovery codes that can never validate, or worse, the storage provider's isValid may still match already-used codes depending on its implementation. The code should remove the credential via the credential manager in a way that also deletes it from federated storage (e.g., user.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById only works locally; a federated-aware removal path is needed), or the logic should account for federated credentials explicitly.

findings.title: getCredential federated-first lookup can return a stale federated credential even when a newer local credential exists
findings.body: getCredential() checks getFederatedCredentialsStream() first and only falls back to local storage if no federated credential is found. If a user previously had recovery codes in federated storage and later a new credential was created locally (or vice versa), the lookup order is fixed and does not consider createdDate or which credential is current. In a mixed scenario (e.g., user migrated, or a credential exists in both stores), the federated one always wins even if it is older or fully consumed, while the local one is ignored. This can cause the login flow to display the wrong code number (RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean) or to fail to remove the correct credential after use. The lookup should prefer the most recently created credential across both stores, or at minimum the callers should be aware that federated credentials take precedence unconditionally.

findings.title: disableCredentialType does not handle recovery-authn-codes type, so federated recovery credentials cannot be disabled
findings.body: disableCredentialType() only handles OTP types (sets myUser.otp = null) and logs 'Unsupported to disable credential of type' for everything else. The recovery-authn-codes type is now supported by this provider (supportsCredentialType, updateCredential, isValid, isConfiguredFor, getCredentials all handle it), but there is no way to disable/remove it. The account console and admin REST 'disable credential type' operations for recovery codes on federated users will silently fail (the provider returns without clearing myUser.recoveryCodes), leaving the credential active. The method should add a branch to null out myUser.recoveryCodes when credentialType equals RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE, and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream should include the recovery codes type when present so the UI offers it.

findings.title: New recovery-codes federation test does not verify that codes are consumed/removed or that a second login with a used code fails
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only verifies setup (credential lands in user storage, no DB credentials) and a single successful login with the first code. It does not verify the security-critical behaviors of the feature: (1) that after using a code, the used code is marked/removed so it cannot be replayed, (2) that logging in again with the same code fails, (3) that after all 12 codes are consumed the credential is removed and the user is prompted to configure new codes (the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action path in RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator), and (4) that the stored credential in user storage is hashed rather than plaintext. Given that the production change introduces a new storage path for these bearer credentials, the absence of a replay/consumption test leaves the most important integrity property untested.
